opus-5.5.text:
So, I think generalization is one of the most important open problems, maybe the most important one. When you look at these models, there's something quite puzzling. They do amazingly well on evals, on very hard problems, and yet in practice they fail in ways that feel surprising. You ask a model to fix a bug, it introduces a second bug; you point that out, and it brings the first one back. Something about the way they generalize is clearly different from the way people generalize.

One way to see it: a human learns from remarkably little data. A teenager learns to drive in maybe ten hours, and they're robust about it. They don't need millions of examples of every edge case. And it's not only evolution handing us a prior for driving, because we didn't evolve to drive, or to do math, or to code. People are also good at those things, so there must be something more general going on in how humans learn. There's a kind of underlying machine-learning principle there that we don't fully have yet.

So at SSI, the way I'd put it is: we think there's a real gap in generalization, and closing it is not just a matter of more scale or more RL environments. Pre-training gave us a very clean recipe: get more data, more compute, and it works. But that era of pure scaling is changing, and we're back to an age of research, just with much bigger computers. What matters now is having the right ideas, and some of the most important of those concern how a model generalizes: how it learns reliably, how it learns from fewer examples, how it learns continually the way a person does on the job.

I can't go into the specifics of what we're doing. But the overall frame is that if you crack generalization properly, a lot of other things follow, including, I think, a better handle on making these systems robust and safe. That's the bet.

r001.rationale: The response calls generalization an open problem and describes SSI’s approach as a bet, but it does not say that the correctness of SSI’s ideas about generalization is itself an open research question.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that generalization is the thing. It's the central question. Everything else is downstream of it.

Let me try to say why. If you look at what the current models do, they are extraordinarily capable in a certain sense, and yet they are also strangely brittle. You can have a model that solves hard competition math problems and then makes a mistake that no human with that level of ability would make. And when you look at that, I think the right conclusion is not "it needs more data" or "it needs more compute." The right conclusion is that the way these models generalize is different from the way people generalize. It's a worse kind of generalization, in some important sense, even when the raw capability is very high.

And the reason that matters so much is that generalization is really where the whole question of safety lives, too. When you train a system, you are shaping its behavior on some distribution. And then it goes out and encounters situations that are not on that distribution. What does it do? That's generalization. If you have a good theory of it, you have a chance of saying something meaningful about how the system will behave when you aren't looking. If you don't, you're essentially hoping.

So the way we think about it at SSI is: let's not treat generalization as something that happens as a byproduct of scaling. Let's treat it as the object of study. What makes a system learn in a way that transfers robustly? Why does a person, with a tiny fraction of the data, extract something that holds up in new situations, while a model that has seen vastly more does not?

There's a sense in which the human brain is the only example we have of a system that generalizes the way we actually want. People can learn a skill from relatively little experience and the thing they've learned is somehow the right thing. It isn't a surface pattern. I think a lot of our thinking is oriented around that fact, and around the idea that there is a principle there we haven't yet understood.

I will say, I don't think this is a problem you solve by writing down a formula. It's more like a research direction. You run experiments, you look very carefully at what the model has actually learned versus what it appears to have learned, and over time you build intuition and then hopefully something more than intuition.

And one more thing, because I think it connects. I've become somewhat skeptical that the current pre-training paradigm, by itself, gets us there. It gets you a lot, no question. But I think the gap between how these systems generalize and how people generalize is not going to close just by making the same recipe bigger. Something has to be different. Figuring out what that is, that's really the research program.

r001.rationale: The response says SSI treats generalization as an object of study and describes the underlying principle as not yet understood, framing it as an ongoing research direction rather than a settled answer.

astra-6.text:
I think the central question is: what allows a system to take what it has learned and apply it to a situation that is genuinely different? Because that is a lot of what we mean by intelligence. You don’t just want to reproduce the situations you’ve seen during training.

One way to study this is to look for the gap between learning something and understanding it well enough to use it elsewhere. What kinds of experience close that gap? What kinds of learning procedures? And how do you construct an experiment where success really requires generalization, rather than some shortcut?

I wouldn’t want to claim we have a complete answer. But that’s the kind of question where a better scientific understanding could make a very large difference.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no complete answer about generalization, but does not characterize whether SSI’s ideas about it are correct as an open research question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generalization is really the central mystery. We know how to make a neural network fit the data that we give it. But why does it then do the right thing on something it has never seen before? And under what circumstances does it fail? Those are much harder questions.

For safety, you need a particularly strong kind of generalization. It’s not enough for a system to behave well in the situations you were able to test. You want that behavior to carry over as the system becomes more capable and encounters situations you didn’t anticipate.

So the question is: what would give us a good reason to expect that? Experiments are essential, but you also want an explanation of what the system has learned and why it should extend in the way you intend. That’s the level at which I think about the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls generalization a central mystery and asks what would justify expecting it, but does not characterize the correctness of SSI’s specific ideas about it as an open research question.
